storeCredit.title: Store Credit Management System
storeCredit.description: A production app that replaced a paper credit ledger with a real-time system the whole store staff relies on daily.
storeCredit.overview: My family runs a small neighborhood grocery store that, like many in Costa Rica, extends informal credit to regular customers, known locally as "fiado". For years that credit was tracked in a paper notebook: illegible handwriting, lost pages, no way to audit who wrote what or when, and no backup if the notebook itself got damaged.
storeCredit.problem: The notebook worked until it didn't. Balances got miscounted, entries got disputed, and there was no way for more than one person to update it at the same time without creating conflicting records. I built this app to solve that specific problem, not to build a generic point-of-sale system.
storeCredit.role: I designed, built and deployed the entire system alone: data model, front end, notification service and infrastructure, based on how the store staff actually work day to day.
storeCredit.architectureIntro: A React client talks to Firebase directly for reads and writes. A separate Node.js service, running continuously with PM2 on a machine at the store, listens for database changes and triggers outbound notifications.
features: Real-time sync: multiple staff members can log sales and payments at the same time and see updates instantly on every device.
A single shared Firebase Authentication account with a PIN-based profile selector, so every action stays tied to a specific person without individual logins.
Full audit trail: nothing is permanently deleted, every record keeps who created or edited it and when, and suspended accounts can be restored.
Daily summary broken down by payment method, with 80mm thermal receipt printing and one-tap copy for WhatsApp.
Automatic WhatsApp and email alerts sent to each customer on every transaction, handled by the separate notification service so the client app never blocks on it.
Automatic daily database backup to Google Cloud Storage.
storeCredit.screenshotsIntro: The real usage flow, with customer names, phone numbers and profile photos blurred. Amounts without an attached name aren't sensitive.

gallery.profileSelector: Profile selector: whoever is on shift picks their name and enters their PIN.
gallery.clientList: Customer list sorted by debt, with the store's total outstanding credit.
gallery.clientDetail: A customer's detail view: current debt, credit limit, history, and the buttons to log a purchase or payment.
gallery.dailySummary: Daily summary by payment method, used to balance the register at closing.
gallery.dailyMovements: Feed of every transaction for the day, in chronological order.

storeCredit.outcome: The app has fully replaced the paper ledger and is used every day by store staff, with zero infrastructure cost since it runs entirely on free-tier services.
storeCredit.stack: React, Vite, Firebase (Realtime Database, Authentication), Node.js, PM2, Vercel with continuous deployment from GitHub, Google Cloud Storage for backups.

alwaysBarca.title: Always Barça
alwaysBarca.description: 33 seasons, five variables, one question: does transfer spending predict FC Barcelona's success better than academy usage, squad value, coaching, or the presidency?
alwaysBarca.question: What actually explains FC Barcelona's successful seasons: how much the club spends, or who is making the decisions? Net transfer spending, coaching continuity, academy usage, squad market value, and the presidency, tested against 33 LaLiga seasons (1993/94–2025/26). The analysis deliberately avoids isolating a single era, coach and president are treated as variables across the full range instead, so both the general pattern and era comparisons stay visible.
alwaysBarca.methodology: Performance is measured both as points earned over the season maximum (normalized across eras) and as a categorical outcome adjusted to a club of Barça's scale. Spending and squad value are expressed as Barça's share of that season's total LaLiga market, not raw euros, since the transfer market has inflated much faster than the economy. Pearson correlation covers the continuous variables; coach and president are categorical, so a one-way ANOVA and its eta-squared (η²) put them on the same explained-variance scale as r². Sources: automated data from football-data.co.uk and Transfermarkt/Kaggle from 2014/15 on, manual collection cross-validated against two site views for 1993/94–2013/14, and hand-built coach/president tables.
findings: Coaching (η² = 0.727) and squad market value (r² = 0.567) explain performance significantly; net spending (r² = 0.052) and academy usage (r² = 0.075) don't.
Guardiola leads average performance (0.818, 3 titles in 4 seasons). Title seasons were won both with near-zero net spending (1997/98, 2025/26) and with heavy investment.
Squad value predicts better than spending because it's an accumulated asset (a "stock"), while net spending is a single summer's movement (a "flow").

Average presidential spending is misleading without context: Gaspart and Laporta spent almost the same share (7.5%) with opposite results, because Laporta inherited two separate financial crises (Gaspart's 2000-01 overspend, then Bartomeu's €1.35B debt in 2021).
2024/25–2025/26 show homegrown talent (Yamal, Gavi, Fermín López, Balde) driving squad value to its highest points in the range while net transfer spending sits near zero.
alwaysBarca.dashboardsIntro: Four linked dashboards on Tableau Public, one per phase of the analysis.

overview.title: Performance, spending & coaching
overview.description: How performance, net transfer spending and coaching changes move together across 33 seasons.

academy.title: Academy usage
academy.description: Minutes played by La Masía academy players per season, and whether that usage correlates with performance.

squadValue.title: Squad value
squadValue.description: Squad market value per season, one of the two statistically significant variables.

conclusions.title: Conclusions
conclusions.description: Pearson correlation and ANOVA results across all five variables, with limitations documented.

alwaysBarca.summaryIntro: Every variable expressed as variance explained: r² for the continuous ones, η² for the categorical ones, the same conceptual quantity.
alwaysBarca.conclusion: Neither spending nor academy usage predicts Barça's performance well across 33 years. Accumulated squad value does, and who is in charge, coach first and president second, explains even more. Confirming this with causal rigor would need comparable data from other clubs, outside this project's scope.
alwaysBarca.limitations: Academy usage and squad value only cover 2012/13 onward (Transfermarkt's coverage isn't reliable before that), so those two variables run on 14 of the 33 seasons, not the full range. "Academy player" also has no single accepted definition, this project uses a broad one (anyone in Wikipedia's La Masía-formed table). One manual correction was applied: 2006/07 initially showed a technical tie with Real Madrid under a simplified standings model, corrected by hand to match the real title (decided by head-to-head tiebreaker). And throughout: correlation isn't causation, especially for the presidency findings, where inherited financial context matters as much as the numbers.
alwaysBarca.personalNote: This project didn't start from a convenient generic dataset, it started from being a culé, writing this from almost 8,970 km away in Alajuela, Costa Rica. It's a fitting moment to close it too, with a new La Masía generation (Yamal, Cubarsí, Fermín López) already showing up in the data.
alwaysBarca.stack: Python and Pandas for data collection and cleaning, SciPy for the statistical tests (Pearson, ANOVA), Tableau Public for the four published dashboards.

messiOutlier.title: Messi: Outlier
messiOutlier.description: How singular is Messi's World Cup profile? Measured against the full population of 5,636 historical World Cup outfield players, not a handful of hand-picked comparisons.
messiOutlier.question: Does any historical World Cup player come close to combining, at the same time, the metrics that separate elite finishers, dribblers, chance creators and play organizers, or does Messi's profile stand out for appearing among the elite of several distinct functional roles at once?
messiOutlier.thesis: "Outlier" can suggest absolute uniqueness, and that's not quite what the data shows. Messi shares the highest ceiling actually observed (elite in 3 of 4 roles) with 7 other players. What holds up under every threshold tested is more precise: no player's profile clearly exceeds or consistently matches his on the measure that matters most, average role percentile among players with a real career-length sample.
approach: Players compared by functional role (finisher, dribbler, chance creator, play organizer), not nominal position. 16 metrics, normalized per 90 minutes, aggregated at player-career level (1966–2026), with a 270-minute floor tested up to 900 and 1,500 as a transparency check.
"Elite" is defined by percentile (90th, 95th, 99th), calculated against the full relevant population, 5,636 outfield players, not a handful of reference names.
The hypothesis was allowed to fail, and did in its strongest form: no player, including Messi, reaches elite status in all four roles at once at a genuine threshold.
messiOutlier.rolesIntro: Functional roles, not fixed pitch positions, since the same player shifts position across a career.

roles.finisher: Finisher — converts chances into goals: goals, xG, shot conversion, shots on target.
roles.unbalancer: Dribbler — creates individual danger by taking on defenders: successful dribbles, fouls drawn, progressive carries.
roles.playmaker: Chance creator — creates the direct chance: assists, key passes, xA, big chances created.
roles.orchestrator: Play organizer — circulates the ball and progresses the attack from deeper zones: progressive passes, completion rate, passes into the final third.

findings: SofaScore's internal API gave comparable event-level detail across the full 1966–2026 range (validated against a 1986 Maradona match and the 2022 final). Full extraction: 900 matches, 5,636 outfield players.
The three attacking roles correlate moderately (0.49–0.58); play organizer is nearly independent (0.02–0.30), a genuinely distinct skill, predicted in advance to be Messi's relative weak point.

No player reaches elite status in all 4 roles at a genuine threshold. The real ceiling, elite in 3 of 4, is shared by 8 players; Messi has by far the largest career sample (6 World Cups, 34 matches, 3,054 minutes) and the highest average role percentile among players with a real career-length sample.

Maradona is a genuine runner-up, the gap explained almost entirely by play organizer, exactly as predicted. Cristiano Ronaldo, with a nearly identical career sample, has the lowest average role score in the comparison set, evidence the finding isn't simply about playing many World Cups.

Building the reference set surfaced its own catch: the base-threshold organizer leader was driven by a single high-volume, low-threat match, not real organizing quality, a stricter 900-minute floor fixed who gets shown as a "leader."
messiOutlier.dashboardsIntro: A 3-part interactive dashboard on Tableau Public.

rolesDistinct.title: Are the four roles really distinct?
rolesDistinct.description: Role correlation heatmap and an interactive scatter of the weakest pair: chance creator vs. play organizer.

centralFinding.title: The central finding
centralFinding.description: Average role score vs. career minutes, with an interactive minimum-minutes control, and how many roles each player reaches at the elite threshold.

profiles.title: Profiles
profiles.description: Messi against the Phase 6 reference set, each role's individual top 5, and an editorially-selected set of historical GOAT candidates.

messiOutlier.conclusion: No player's profile in the 1966–2026 World Cup population clearly exceeds or consistently matches Messi's across the four roles measured here, tested across multiple percentile thresholds and minimum-minutes floors, none of which changed the result. The one relative weakness found, play organizer, was predicted before the data was ever run, which strengthens the finding rather than undermining it. The declared limitation stands: this measures roughly 6 months of accumulated football against a much longer career, a deliberate scope choice, not an oversight.
messiOutlier.closingTitle: Closing a chapter, while this project was closing too
messiOutlier.closing: On August 31, 2026, while this project was in the middle of being built, Lionel Messi officially announced his retirement from the Argentina national team, after playing his sixth World Cup. At 39, in what turned out to be his last tournament, he scored 8 goals and gave 4 assists in 8 matches, taking Argentina to the final. His World Cup story is closed for good: six tournaments between 2006 and 2026, 34 matches, 21 goals. This wasn't planned, the project started as a portfolio exercise and ended up coinciding with the real, final close of the career it analyzes. Thank you, Leo. And I will always carry December 18, 2022 in my heart, the day you fulfilled your childhood dream.
dataSources: SofaScore — the project's sole data source, match-level stats accessed through its internal API (no official public API exists), via the ScraperFC library.
FBref and Kaggle were considered as complementary sources but weren't ultimately needed.
messiOutlier.stack: Python, Pandas, Jupyter Notebook and Matplotlib for the analysis, ScraperFC for SofaScore extraction, Tableau Public for the 3-part dashboard.

batazo.title: Batazo: football prediction pools for friends
batazo.description: Batazo is a football prediction pool web app for groups of friends. I'm building it with .NET 10 and React, in phases, documenting every decision along the way.
batazo.statusNote: This project is under active development. The technical foundation and deployment are done; the pool features come in the next phase, and I'll keep this page updated as I go.
batazo.overview: My friends and I run prediction pools, and the apps we were using don't cover Costa Rica's Primera División. The few that do weren't good enough for us, so we ended up spread across several apps depending on the league. Batazo puts everything in one place: major leagues with automatic results, the local league, and custom pools the group sets up itself with results entered by hand.
batazo.name: It comes from "batear", Costa Rican slang for stating something as fact without actually knowing it, basically taking a wild guess. Which is exactly what you do when you predict a match.
batazo.problem: A small group needs a private pool where everyone predicts the score before kickoff, nobody can change it afterwards or peek at other people's picks too early, and the standings update on their own. It also has to work with competitions no API covers, like the Costa Rican league or a tournament the friends made up. It only tracks points: no money, no betting.
batazo.roleTitle: My role and how I work
batazo.role: It's a personal project I'm building on my own. The main goal is to get back into backend development with C# and .NET, and to have a real system in my portfolio: its own API, a relational database, authentication, an external service integration, tests, and continuous deployment. I use AI as a tutor and reviewer, not as the author: I write the code myself, work in small steps, test each one before moving on, and don't commit anything I can't explain. I track work on a Jira Kanban board, with one branch and one pull request per task, and keep a technical decision log in the repo.
batazo.architectureIntro: It's a layered monolith deployed as a single app. ASP.NET Core serves the API under /api and the React build too, so everything lives on the same domain: no CORS setup, and session cookies just work. The solution has a domain project (business rules, no dependency on the database or external services), an infrastructure project (EF Core), and an API project. Since Render's free tier puts the server to sleep without traffic, result syncing won't run in the background: a scheduled GitHub Actions workflow will call an internal endpoint that runs it.

architectureSteps.label: Browser running React, served by ASP.NET Core
ASP.NET Core API under /api (only a test endpoint for now)
EF Core and PostgreSQL on Neon
Scheduled GitHub Actions calls the internal sync endpoint

decisions: 5, 3, 1, 0 scoring: exact score, correct winner and goal difference, correct outcome only, or a miss. Predicting 1-1 when it ends 0-0 earns 3, since you got both the draw and the goal difference. Every app I looked at uses three tiers, and this one is easy to explain to the group.
Predictions lock at kickoff, enforced on the server, never just in the browser. Once a match has started, its predictions never reopen, even if it gets rescheduled.
Other people's predictions show up once the match is over. That way nobody copies or tweaks their pick based on someone else's during the game.

In knockout matches, the 90-minute score counts. football-data.org folds penalties into the final score (a 1-1 decided 6-5 on penalties shows up as 7-6), so the provider has to read the regular-time field.

One API (football-data.org, starting with LaLiga) and everything else entered manually, including the Costa Rican league. The API that does cover it limits its free tier to old seasons, and one well-built integration shows the same skills as two. Each source sits behind an interface, so another one can be added without touching the rest.

Login through ASP.NET Core Identity with an HttpOnly cookie, no custom tokens. Password reset uses Identity's token sent by email, and responds the same way whether or not the account exists, so it doesn't leak which emails are registered.

Every API error uses ProblemDetails (RFC 9457) with a trace ID, and validation messages come in Spanish straight from the backend. The frontend only has to handle one error format, and an error a user sees can be traced in the logs.
done: Layered .NET 10 solution with centralized package versions and warnings treated as errors.
PostgreSQL with EF Core, migrations applied on startup, snake_case naming.
ProblemDetails error contract, input validation with Spanish messages, and a /health check.
JSON logs in production and configuration validated at startup.
Injectable clock (TimeProvider), with an analyzer that bans reading the system time directly.
Multi-stage Docker image running as non-root.
GitHub Actions CI (backend and frontend) required to merge into main, and automatic deployment to Render with the database on Neon, only when CI passes.
React frontend with strict TypeScript, a typed HTTP client that understands the API's errors, and TanStack Query set up.
next: Finish the frontend foundation: public and protected routes, plus loading, error, and empty state components.
Accounts: sign-up, login, and password reset by email.
Teams, competitions, matchdays, and matches entered manually.
Predictions with cutoff, results with an audit log, scoring, and overall standings, with unit tests for each rule.
After that: integration tests, CSV import and team crests, and automatic results from football-data.org.
lessons: Validation in .NET: with a positional record, validation attributes end up on the constructor parameter, and error keys came out with the C# name ("Message") instead of the JSON name ("message"). I switched input DTOs to records with init properties so the frontend could highlight the right field. I also dropped C#'s required modifier, because the error surfaced as a parsing failure without the Spanish message.
CI kept failing on "dotnet format" because of the migrations EF Core generates. I fixed it by marking them as generated code instead of reformatting them by hand every time.

Twice I ended up committing straight to main because I hadn't created the branch first. I moved the commits to a branch and added a fixed step to check the current branch before starting each task. main is also protected now: it only changes through a pull request with green CI.
batazo.stack: C# with .NET 10, ASP.NET Core Web API, Entity Framework Core with Npgsql, PostgreSQL (Docker locally, Neon in production), React with TypeScript and Vite, TanStack Query, Docker, GitHub Actions, and Render.
